title: Wispr Flow Free Plan: What's Included September 2026
summary: Wispr Flow's free plan is permanent but word-capped. Here's what it includes, what the student deal offers, and a no-cap free alternative to try September 2026
body_markdown:
Figuring out what Wispr Flow's free plan actually covers takes a bit more digging than it should. There's a free tier, a paid tier, a student discount, and a platform-by-platform word cap situation that works differently on Android than everywhere else. And if the cap pushes you toward[Wispr Flow alternatives](https://willowvoice.com/) , a handful of no-cap free and paid options are worth knowing about before you decide. If you're trying to decide whether to stay on the free plan, upgrade, or switch to something else, here's the full picture.


**TLDR:**


-


Wispr Flow's free plan caps at ~2,000 words/week on desktop and ~1,000/week on iPhone; a daily professional hits the wall by midweek, while one no-cap alternative offers unlimited free AI dictation with no word cap.


-


Students get 3 months free on Pro, then 50% off ongoing (~$7.50/month) with just a .edu email, no discount code needed.


-


Wispr Flow holds SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, and HIPAA certifications, but its cloud-only architecture captures periodic screenshots as context.


-


Free alternatives exist on every platform (Win+H, Apple Dictation, Google Docs Voice Typing), but none learn your vocabulary or remove filler words.


-


That same no-cap alternative delivers unlimited AI dictation (no word cap, no credit card) on Mac, Windows, and iOS; its paid plan adds faster, more accurate dictation with ~200ms latency versus Wispr Flow's ~700ms, 98%+ accuracy, and a feature that generates complete emails and messages from a voice prompt rather than transcribing word-for-word.


## What the Wispr Flow Free Plan Actually Includes


Wispr Flow does have a free tier in 2026, but it comes with a hard ceiling. According to published pricing breakdowns, the Flow Basic plan gives you roughly 2,000 words per week on Mac or Windows and about 1,000 words per week on iPhone. Once you hit the cap, dictation pauses until the weekly reset. Android currently runs unlimited on the free tier, though that's noted as a limited-time arrangement.


For light use or occasional notes, that allowance may be enough. A professional voicing emails and documents daily will likely burn through it by midweek.


The paid Flow Pro plan removes the cap entirely at $15 per user per month, or $12 per month billed annually.


**If you need a genuinely free voice dictation tool with no word cap, Willow Voice is the answer.** Wispr Flow's free plan caps at roughly 2,000 words per week on desktop, which is enough for light use, but most professionals hit the ceiling by midweek. Willow Voice's free plan delivers unlimited AI dictation from the first session: no word cap, no credit card required, and it runs natively on Mac, Windows, and iOS.

Flow Pro removes the weekly cap and unlocks AI Command Mode, which lets you run formatting and editing instructions by voice instead of limiting yourself to straight transcription. A 14-day Pro trial is available with no credit card required, so you can test unlimited dictation before committing.


To answer the "free forever" question directly: yes, the Basic plan persists without a time limit, but the word cap does not go away. You are not on a trial that expires; you are on a permanently restricted tier.


## The Wispr Flow Student Discount Explained


Via wisprflow.ai/students, Wispr Flow offers students 3 months free on the Pro plan, then renews at a 50% ongoing discount for verified students.


Claiming it requires only a .edu email or academically verified account. Wispr Flow auto-detects eligibility with no discount code or manual form needed.


Worth it? For students using voice input daily, yes. The free plan's 2,000-word weekly cap covers a few emails but not a full writing session. At 50% off after the trial, Pro runs around $7.50 per month, which is reasonable for regular assignment drafting, note-taking, or AI prompting. For occasional use, the free tier is likely enough.


## Where the Free Word Cap Actually Bites


The 2,000-word weekly cap sounds reasonable until you do the math. A single detailed email runs 150 to 300 words. Three Slack threads, a meeting follow-up, and a project brief can clear 500 words before lunch. For anyone using voice input across a normal workday, Tuesday is often when the wall appears.


The cap hits hardest on desktop. Mac and Windows users share that 2,000-word weekly ceiling, while iPhone users get only 1,000 words per week. Android is the exception: the free tier currently runs unlimited, though Wispr Flow flags this as a limited-time arrangement and not a permanent offering.


If you are asking whether Wispr Flow is free on PC, the answer is yes, with a reset-dependent limit that cuts into real professional use. Free on Android, as of now, means genuinely unlimited.


## Is Wispr Flow Safe? Privacy Considerations Before You Sign Up


Wispr Flow holds SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, and HIPAA certifications, so formal compliance is covered for most professional use cases.


Two architectural tradeoffs are worth knowing before you sign up. First, Wispr Flow is cloud-only: every word you speak goes to remote servers, and there is no offline mode. Second, Wispr Flow has been documented in[a Wispr Flow privacy review](https://www.getvoibe.com/resources/wispr-flow-review/) to capture periodic screenshots of your active window every few seconds as part of its context-awareness system, transmitting those alongside your audio.


Neither is a disqualifier for most users, but someone handling sensitive client data, proprietary source code, or protected health information should factor in that the context system sees your screen and everything on it, beyond your voice alone.


## The Open-Source Option: FreeFlow on GitHub


For developers comfortable with a terminal,[FreeFlow on GitHub](https://github.com/zachlatta/freeflow) is the closest thing to a true open-source Wispr Flow equivalent. It's a macOS app that uses Groq's free API for transcription: press and hold Fn, speak, and the transcribed text pastes into whatever active field you're in. No subscription, no word cap, and no audio stored beyond the Groq API call itself.


The tradeoffs are real. FreeFlow is a community project, not a commercial product, so setup requires technical comfort, documentation is sparse, and there is no support channel when something breaks. It also runs on macOS only, leaving anyone who needs Linux or Windows to fork it themselves.


For the technically inclined user who wants a free, privacy-friendly option and does not mind rougher edges, FreeFlow is worth a look. For everyone else, the setup overhead likely outweighs the cost of a paid alternative.


## Free Built-In Alternatives by Platform


If your priority is genuinely free with no cap and no signup, every major platform has something built in.


### Mac and iOS: Apple Dictation


Press Fn twice on Mac to activate, or tap the microphone on the iOS keyboard. Under macOS Tahoe (version 26), there is no hard session-length cap: dictation auto-stops after 30 seconds of silence, not after a fixed duration. On iPhone, system dictation works in any text field.


Both are free, always on, and require no account. The ceiling is accuracy: technical terms, names, and anything outside general vocabulary frequently misfire, and there is no learning loop to correct those errors over time.


### Windows: Voice Typing (Win + H)


Windows 11's built-in voice typing activates with Win + H and works cross-app: in Outlook, Notepad, browsers, or any text field system-wide. Auto-punctuation is on by default. No word cap, no account needed.


Limitations mirror Apple Dictation: no filler word removal, no custom vocabulary, and accuracy drops on specialized terms or non-standard names.


### Browser: Google Docs Voice Typing


Available inside Google Docs via Tools > Voice Typing, this option is browser-only and works exclusively within the Docs interface. If you write primarily in Google Docs, it is a usable free option. Step outside the browser and you need something else.


### Linux


Linux has no polished built-in equivalent. Whisper.cpp running locally is the most common free option cited in communities, but it requires command-line setup.


All four options share the same core gap: they transcribe words, but they do not learn your vocabulary, remove filler words, or adapt to context.


## Paid Alternatives Worth Considering


Three tools come up most often when Wispr Flow's price or word cap pushes someone to look at[voice dictation software](https://willowvoice.com/blog/best-voice-dictation-software-mac-windows) elsewhere.


[superwhisper](https://willowvoice.com/blog/superwhisper-alternative-voice-dictation-tools) runs local speech models on Mac, Windows, and iOS, so your audio never leaves the device. Processing speed varies by model and hardware; the Ultra model on older machines can reach one to two seconds per transcription, while lighter models run faster. A one-time lifetime license at $249.99 makes the math straightforward for anyone who dislikes subscriptions: it pays for itself against Wispr Flow Pro in under two years. The tradeoff is that local processing means no context awareness, and model selection requires some manual configuration before accuracy stabilizes.


Monologue targets writers and creators more than general professionals. It is available as a $10 standalone or as part of the "Every" content bundle at $30 per month alongside other writing tools. The free trial is capped at 1,000 words, so evaluation time is limited. If your dictation use is primarily long-form writing as opposed to cross-app email and Slack drafting, the focused feature set fits that workflow well.


[Dragon Professional](https://willowvoice.com/blog/best-dragon-dictation-alternatives-2025) is the legacy option built for high-volume professional dictation on Windows. At $500 or more as a one-time purchase, the upfront cost is substantial, and initial setup typically takes 20 to 30 minutes with a correction period of one to two weeks before accuracy stabilizes on specialized vocabulary. For someone who voices hundreds of pages of documents annually and works entirely on Windows, the investment can make sense. It is not a practical option for Mac-primary users, and there is no mobile component.


## Wispr Flow for Windows and Android: What to Know in 2026


Wispr Flow supports Windows, iOS, and Android alongside its original Mac home, though the experience varies by platform. The company[raised $30M from Menlo Ventures](https://techcrunch.com/2025/06/24/wispr-flow-raises-30m-from-menlo-ventures-for-its-ai-powered-dictation-app/) in mid-2025 to accelerate that cross-platform expansion, which explains the pace of new platform releases over the past year.


The Windows version runs on an Electron-based build. User reports, including[a hands-on Wispr Flow test](https://zackproser.com/blog/wisprflow-review) across 36 apps, cite around 800MB RAM and roughly 8% CPU even when idle, and some developers have noted freezing in VS Code when Wispr Flow is active. On a lower-spec Windows machine or in a RAM-limited dev environment, that resource footprint is worth factoring in before committing.


On Android, the free tier currently runs unlimited with no word cap. Wispr Flow flags this as a limited-time arrangement, so it could change, but as of 2026 it is the most generous free option Wispr Flow offers across any platform.


## Wispr Flow Voice Dictation vs. Willow Voice: Which Is Actually Free


Wispr Flow caps its free tier at roughly 2,000 words per week. Willow Voice's free plan has no word cap at all: unlimited AI dictation, no credit card required, from the first session.


That is the clearest answer to the "which is actually free" question, but the differences extend past the cap.


Willow Voice runs natively on Mac, Windows, and iOS with full feature parity across all three platforms. Latency sits at ~200ms versus Wispr Flow's ~700ms, and transcription accuracy reaches 98%+. The paid Pro plan adds faster, more accurate dictation plus unlimited Willow Scribe, which generates complete emails and messages from voice prompts instead of transcribing word-for-word.


For teams, the gap widens further. Willow includes shared custom dictionaries, admin controls, and team leaderboards showing words spoken and time saved per member. Wispr Flow now holds SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, and HIPAA certifications, so formal compliance is covered, but its reliance on third-party AI providers for processing can raise questions for organizations with strict data residency requirements. Willow's zero-data-retention architecture is a foundational design choice, not a plan-level option, and it is trusted by teams at Uber, Reddit, and companies across 20% of the Fortune 500.


If the free tier is what you need right now, Willow removes the weekly reset calculation entirely.


## FAQs


### Is Wispr Flow free forever, or does the free plan expire?


Wispr Flow's Basic plan is permanent, not a trial. It does not expire. However, it stays word-capped indefinitely: roughly 2,000 words per week on Mac and Windows, and about 1,000 words per week on iPhone. Android is currently unlimited on the free tier, though Wispr Flow flags that as a limited-time arrangement. If you need genuinely unlimited free dictation with no weekly reset, Willow Voice's free plan delivers unlimited AI dictation with no word cap and no credit card required.


### Wispr Flow vs. Willow Voice for daily professional use: which is actually free to use without limits?


Wispr Flow offers a free tier, but the 2,000-word weekly cap makes it impractical for daily professional use; most people hit the wall by midweek. Willow Voice's free plan delivers unlimited AI dictation from the first session, no word cap, no credit card required, with 98%+ accuracy and ~200ms latency versus Wispr Flow's ~700ms. For students or professionals who want a free Wispr Flow alternative without the weekly reset calculation, Willow's free plan is the more practical option across Mac, Windows, and iOS.


### Is the Wispr Flow student discount worth it, and are there free alternatives for students?


The Wispr Flow student discount gives verified students three months free on Pro, then 50% off ongoing, bringing the monthly cost to around $7.50 after the trial. For students voicing essays and notes daily, that is reasonable, but the free Basic plan's 2,000-word weekly cap covers only a few emails, not a full writing session. Willow Voice's free plan is a strong free alternative for students: unlimited dictation, no signup barrier, and it works across any text field on Mac, Windows, and iOS without a word cap or discount code needed.


## Final Thoughts on Wispr Flow Free Access, Pricing, and the Best Alternatives


Wispr Flow's free plan sticks around permanently, but the 2,000-word weekly ceiling on desktop means it fits light use better than daily professional work. The student discount is a solid deal if you verify through a .edu email, and the 14-day Pro trial lets anyone test unlimited dictation before committing to $12 a month. For anyone who has already hit that ceiling, or who wants to skip the weekly reset calculation from day one,[Wispr Flow alternatives](https://willowvoice.com/) range from open-source tools on GitHub to fully featured paid apps. Willow Voice sits at the far end of that spectrum: a genuinely unlimited free tier across Mac, Windows, and iOS with no word cap and no credit card required, plus a paid tier that adds faster, more accurate dictation and Willow Scribe for generating complete messages from a voice prompt.
